title: Latent variables & mixtures
blurb: Hidden factors, Gaussian mixtures as shallow LVMs, clustering via the posterior

hook.title: The chef’s secret recipe
hook.text: You taste dishes ($x$), but you never see the chef's **secret recipe card** ($z$): cuisine, spice level, cooking time. Those hidden choices explain all the variation you taste. A photo is the same: pixels vary because of gender, eye colour, hair colour, pose, but nobody wrote those factors down, they are **latent**. If you could guess the recipe card, predicting the dish would be easy (the “$p(x|z)$ is simpler than $p(x)$” idea). Guessing the card from the dish, $p(z|x)$, is the hard direction.
hook.recall: Remember the chef’s recipe card: $z$ is hidden, $x$ is what you taste. Generating goes card → dish ($p(x|z)$); clustering goes dish → card ($p(z|x)$).

explore.intro: A mixture of three Gaussians: first pick a component $z$, then draw $x$ from it. Colours show the hidden $z$.
tasks: Click inside a clump, then between two clumps. How does $p(z|x)$ change?
Raise the spread σ. What happens to the posterior in the overlap region?
explore.takeaway: Mixture of Gaussians: $z\sim\text{Categorical}$, $p(x|z=k)=\mathcal N(\mu_k,\Sigma_k)$. The posterior $p(z|x)$ identifies the component, clustering from unlabeled data.

build.explanation: Slides 8–9: $z\sim\text{Categorical}(1..K)$, $p(x|z=k)=\mathcal N(\mu_k,\Sigma_k)$, and “the posterior $p(z|x)$ identifies the mixture component.”

questions.prompt: In an image dataset, which of these are **latent** variables (not recorded in the data)?
options: Factors such as eye colour, hair colour and pose
questions.explanation: Only the pixels $x$ are observed; the factors of variation $z$ must be inferred (the chef’s recipe).

questions.prompt: Generative process of a mixture of Gaussians:
options: Pick a component $z$ by sampling, then sample $x$ from that Gaussian

questions.prompt: Prior weights $p(z{=}1)=0.3$, $p(z{=}2)=0.7$. At a point $x$ the component densities are $\mathcal N_1(x)=0.2$ and $\mathcal N_2(x)=0.1$. Find $p(z{=}1\mid x)$ (3 decimals).
questions.explanation: Bayes: $\frac{0.3\cdot0.2}{0.3\cdot0.2+0.7\cdot0.1}=\frac{0.06}{0.13}\approx0.462$. Even though component 1 explains $x$ better, the prior favours component 2.

options: If $z$ is chosen properly, $p(x|z)$ could be much simpler than $p(x)$
In a deep LVM $p(x|z)=\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(z),\Sigma_\theta(z))$ with neural networks $\mu_\theta,\Sigma_\theta$
The conditionals $p(z|x)$ for images are easy to specify by hand
Latent variables are never observed in the training data
questions.explanation: Slide 6: the challenge is that it’s very difficult to specify these conditionals by hand: guessing the recipe card is hard.

questions.prompt: *“A mixture of Gaussians is supervised learning, because it outputs cluster labels.”* What’s the flaw?
options: It is unsupervised: it learns from unlabeled data, and the labels $z$ are latent
Supervised learning has no latent variables
questions.explanation: No one gave the model recipe cards; it infers them.

questions.prompt: Why is the posterior $p(z|x)$ useful for a mixture model?
options: It tells which component most likely produced the data point (clustering)
questions.explanation: Dish → card: which recipe likely made this dish?
